blocks.text: The tokenization pipeline is the final processing step that converts formatted, human readable dataset examples into the numeric token IDs a model actually trains on, handling truncation, padding, attention masks, and label masking along the way.

Even a perfectly clean, well formatted dataset can produce a poorly trained model if this last step is handled carelessly, since it directly determines exactly what numeric signal the model receives during every training step.
1. Where Tokenization Fits in Dataset Preparation

blocks.alt: Formatted text passes through a tokenizer to produce token IDs

blocks.text: Tokenization happens after formatting, and after a chat template has been applied for conversational data, taking the final flat text representation of each example and converting it into the sequence of numeric IDs the model architecture actually operates on.
2. From Raw Text to Token IDs

blocks.alt: A raw string breaks into subword units, which map to integer IDs

blocks.text: Most modern tokenizers break text into subword units, pieces smaller than a full word but often larger than a single character, each mapped to a unique integer ID from the model fixed vocabulary.
This subword approach lets a model handle rare or unseen words gracefully, breaking them into familiar smaller pieces rather than failing entirely on anything outside a fixed whole word vocabulary.
3. Special Tokens Inserted During Tokenization

blocks.alt: A beginning of sequence token and an end of sequence token bracket the content

blocks.text: Beyond the content tokens themselves, tokenization typically inserts special tokens marking the start and end of a sequence, and, for chat formatted data, the role and turn boundary tokens covered in the earlier Chat Templates topic.
4. Truncation, What Happens When Text Is Too Long

blocks.alt: A sequence too long for the limit gets truncated to fit

blocks.text: Every model has a maximum sequence length it can process, and any example that tokenizes to more tokens than that limit needs to be truncated, cutting off content, usually from one end, to fit within the limit.

Truncation applied carelessly can silently cut off the actual answer in a training example, which is why checking the length distribution of a dataset before training, mentioned in the earlier Dataset Formatting topic, matters so much.
5. Padding, Making Batches the Same Length

blocks.alt: A short example gets padding added to match the length of the rest of its batch

blocks.text: Since training processes examples in batches, and most training frameworks require every example in a batch to have the same length, shorter examples get padded with a special padding token to match the length of the longest example in that batch.

code.content:
# A simplified tokenization step with padding and truncation
tokenized = tokenizer(
    formatted_text,
    max_length=2048,
    truncation=True,
    padding="max_length"
)

blocks.text: 6. Attention Masks, Telling the Model What to Ignore

blocks.alt: Real tokens get an attention mask of one while padding tokens get a mask of zero

blocks.text: Alongside the token IDs themselves, an attention mask marks which positions are real content and which are just padding, so the model attention mechanism, covered in the Foundation Models module, knows to ignore the padded positions entirely rather than treating them as meaningful input.

blocks.text: 7. Label Masking for Supervised Fine-Tuning

blocks.alt: Prompt tokens get their labels masked while response tokens keep an active label for computing loss

blocks.text: For supervised fine-tuning, an additional masking step marks which tokens the model should actually be trained to predict, typically the response or completion portion, while the prompt portion is masked out of the loss calculation entirely, echoing the loss masking idea introduced in the Prompt Completion Format topic.

blocks.title: Getting label masking wrong is a subtle, damaging bug
blocks.content: If the prompt tokens are accidentally included in the loss calculation instead of masked out, the model spends training capacity learning to reproduce input it was already given, rather than focusing entirely on generating the correct response.

blocks.text: 8. Pre-Tokenizing vs Tokenizing on the Fly

Tokenization can either happen once ahead of time, saving the tokenized result to disk, or on the fly during each training run, tokenizing each batch as it is loaded. Pre-tokenizing trades disk space and a preprocessing step for faster training start and repeated runs, while on the fly tokenization is simpler to set up but repeats the same work every run.
9. Verifying the Tokenization Pipeline Before a Full Run

Before launching a full training run, decoding a few tokenized examples back into text and visually confirming they match the original formatted input, with the expected special tokens and correct label masking, catches pipeline bugs far earlier and cheaper than discovering them after a long training run finishes with strange results.
Worked Example

A team notices their fine-tuned model seems to just repeat parts of the prompt back rather than generating a genuinely new response. Investigating the tokenization pipeline, they find their label masking step was misconfigured, leaving the prompt tokens included in the loss calculation instead of masked out.

After fixing the masking logic so loss is computed only on the completion tokens, and retraining, the model behavior corrects itself, generating genuinely new responses rather than echoing the prompt, confirming the bug was in the tokenization pipeline rather than the underlying dataset.
Common Mistakes

items: Truncating sequences without checking whether the cut removes the actual target response
Forgetting to mask the prompt portion out of the loss calculation, wasting training signal
Never decoding a tokenized example back to text to visually verify the pipeline is working correctly
Choosing a maximum sequence length far larger than the dataset actually needs, wasting compute on unnecessary padding

blocks.text: Practice

If you have access to a tokenizer for any model, tokenize a short formatted example by hand, then decode the resulting token IDs back to text, and check that the result matches your original input exactly.
Key Takeaway

The tokenization pipeline turns formatted text into the numeric IDs, attention masks, and label masks a model actually trains on, and small mistakes here, incorrect truncation, missing label masking, mismatched special tokens, can silently undermine an otherwise carefully prepared dataset, which is why verifying this final step before a full training run matters as much as the data preparation steps that came before it.
